_about: Editorial assessment by the Afterempire project of the influences on each country's first post-independence economic system (roughly the first two decades). Shares sum to 100 and are judgements drawn from the cited sources, not measurements. Review flags go in the review field.

GBR.name: United Kingdom, c.1945–65
GBR.note: Nationalisation of 'commanding heights' under Attlee without a binding plan; Treasury-led demand management; indicative planning only from the National Economic Development Council (1962). Colonies held sterling balances in the Sterling Area through currency boards.

FRA.name: France, c.1946–65
FRA.note: Indicative planning through the Commissariat général du Plan (Monnet Plan, 1946); FIDES funds carried planned investment to the colonies; franc zone and CFA franc (1945).

PRT.name: Portugal, c.1953–74
PRT.note: Estado Novo corporatism with Planos de Fomento (from 1953) covering metropole and overseas provinces; escudo zone.

NLD.name: Netherlands, c.1945–62
NLD.note: Centraal Planbureau (1945, Tinbergen): macroeconomic forecasting and policy advice rather than directive plans; guilder-linked colonial currencies.

SUN.name: Soviet model
SUN.note: Gosplan five-year plans, state ownership, non-convertible currency, bloc trade.

USA.name: United States / Bretton Woods model
USA.note: Market allocation with project-based aid; after 1980 the World Bank and IMF adjustment agenda (liberalised trade and prices, floating or flexible exchange rates).

IND.summary: A British administrative and legal frame carrying a planning model borrowed largely from the Soviet Union and from India's own pre-independence plans.

notes.text: The Bombay Plan, drafted by Indian industrialists, already called for state-led heavy industry and planned investment.
notes.src: Thakurdas, P. et al. (1944) A Brief Memorandum Outlining a Plan of Economic Development for India

notes.text: Planning Commission set up under the Prime Minister; the First Five-Year Plan (1951) is largely a public investment programme.
notes.src: Government of India, First Five Year Plan (1952)

notes.text: The Second Plan follows P. C. Mahalanobis's two-sector model, prioritising heavy industry in the Soviet manner.
notes.src: Mahalanobis, P. C. (1955) The approach of operational research to planning in India, Sankhyā 16

notes.text: Balance-of-payments crisis and IMF programme; the Eighth Plan (1992) moves to indicative planning.
notes.src: Government of India, Eighth Five Year Plan (1992)

notes.text: Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog, a policy think tank without allocative powers.
notes.src: Government of India Cabinet Resolution, 1 January 2015

PAK.summary: Inherited the Indian civil service and planning-commission form, but its early plans were drafted with US technical advisers.

notes.text: First Five-Year Plan prepared with the Harvard Advisory Group, funded by the Ford Foundation.
notes.src: Papanek, G. (1967) Pakistan's Development: Social Goals and Private Incentives

notes.text: Ayub Khan era: private-sector-led industrialisation steered by the Planning Commission and import licensing.
notes.src: Government of Pakistan, Second Five Year Plan 1960–65

notes.text: Bhutto nationalises banks and heavy industry.
notes.src: Noman, O. (1988) The Political Economy of Pakistan 1947–85

BGD.summary: Began with nationalisation and a socialist-leaning first plan, then moved under donor influence towards liberalisation.

notes.text: Mass nationalisation of industry and banks after independence.
notes.src: Sobhan, R. and Ahmad, M. (1980) Public Enterprise in an Intermediate Regime

notes.text: First Five Year Plan 1973–78 drafted by the Planning Commission under Nurul Islam.
notes.src: Islam, N. (1977) Development Planning in Bangladesh

notes.text: Denationalisation under donor-supported adjustment.
notes.src: World Bank country reports, 1980s

LKA.summary: Swung between welfare-state planning and liberalisation; a British-style state with alternating left and right governments.

notes.text: National Planning Council's Ten-Year Plan.
notes.src: National Planning Council (1959) The Ten-Year Plan

notes.text: United Front government nationalises plantations and expands controls.
notes.src: Five-Year Plan 1972–76

notes.text: Jayewardene government liberalises trade, one of the first in South Asia.
notes.src: Athukorala, P. and Jayasuriya, S. (1994) Macroeconomic Policies, Crises and Growth in Sri Lanka 1969–90

MMR.summary: An American-drafted welfare plan in the 1950s, then an inward-looking military socialism of its own design.

notes.text: Pyidawtha eight-year plan drafted with the US engineering firm Knappen Tippetts Abbett.
notes.src: Government of Burma (1954) Pyidawtha: The New Burma

notes.text: Revolutionary Council publishes The Burmese Way to Socialism; nationalisation follows in 1963.
notes.src: Revolutionary Council (1962) The Burmese Way to Socialism

MYS.summary: Colonial-era development plans carried into independent Malaya; after 1969 a homegrown programme of ethnic economic restructuring.

notes.text: Draft Development Plan of the Federation of Malaya under British rule.
notes.src: Federation of Malaya (1950) Draft Development Plan

notes.text: Economic Planning Unit created in the Prime Minister's Department.
notes.src: Economic Planning Unit history

notes.text: New Economic Policy launched in the Second Malaysia Plan after the 1969 riots.
notes.src: Government of Malaysia, Second Malaysia Plan 1971–75

SGP.summary: A British legal and administrative frame with a homegrown developmental state built around the Economic Development Board.

notes.text: UN industrial survey mission led by Albert Winsemius recommends export-oriented industrialisation.
notes.src: United Nations (1961) A Proposed Industrialization Programme for the State of Singapore

notes.text: Economic Development Board founded; State Development Plan 1961–64.
notes.src: State of Singapore, Development Plan 1961–1964

IDN.summary: Little Dutch planning tradition was carried over; Guided Economy planning under Sukarno, then US-trained technocrats under Suharto.

notes.text: Eight-Year Overall Development Plan under Guided Democracy.
notes.src: Depernas (1961) Rentjana Pembangunan Nasional Semesta Berentjana

notes.text: Repelita I prepared by Bappenas under Widjojo Nitisastro and other Berkeley-trained economists.
notes.src: Thee Kian Wie (ed.) (2003) Recollections: The Indonesian Economy 1950s–1990s

VNM.summary: Soviet-style central planning in the North, extended nationwide after 1976, then the Đổi Mới market transition.

notes.text: First Five-Year Plan of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.
notes.src: DRV, First Five-Year Plan 1961–65

notes.text: Sixth Party Congress adopts Đổi Mới (renovation), opening to markets.
notes.src: Communist Party of Vietnam, Sixth National Congress documents (1986)

GHA.summary: British colonial development plans continued at first; Nkrumah's Seven-Year Plan turned socialist, before IMF-backed recovery in 1983.

notes.text: Colonial First Development Plan; Second Development Plan 1959–64 begun before independence.
notes.src: Killick, T. (1978) Development Economics in Action

notes.text: Seven-Year Development Plan aims at a socialist transformation, with state enterprises and Eastern-bloc ties.
notes.src: Government of Ghana (1964) Seven-Year Plan for National Reconstruction and Development

notes.text: Economic Recovery Programme with the IMF and World Bank.
notes.src: Government of Ghana (1983) Economic Recovery Programme

NGA.summary: Federal development plans in the British mould, an oil-financed state expansion in the 1970s, then structural adjustment.

notes.text: First National Development Plan 1962–68.
notes.src: Federal Government of Nigeria (1962) National Development Plan 1962–68

notes.text: Indigenisation decree and the Second National Development Plan expand the public sector.
notes.src: Federal Government of Nigeria (1970) Second National Development Plan 1970–74

notes.text: Structural Adjustment Programme.
notes.src: Federal Government of Nigeria (1986) SAP

KEN.summary: 'African socialism' in name, a market economy with planning in practice, close to the late-colonial model.

notes.text: Sessional Paper No. 10 defines African socialism while protecting private property and foreign investment.
notes.src: Republic of Kenya (1965) Sessional Paper No. 10

notes.text: World Bank structural adjustment lending.
notes.src: World Bank (1980s) Kenya structural adjustment loans

TZA.summary: A largely homegrown socialism (ujamaa), with Chinese and Nordic support, reversed under IMF-backed recovery from 1986.

notes.text: The Arusha Declaration commits Tanzania to socialism and self-reliance; banks and major firms nationalised.
notes.src: Nyerere, J. (1967) The Arusha Declaration

notes.text: Villagisation programme.
notes.src: Coulson, A. (1982) Tanzania: A Political Economy

notes.text: Economic Recovery Programme with the IMF.
notes.src: Government of Tanzania (1986) ERP

SEN.summary: French-style plan ministry, CFA franc and French technical advisers; Mamadou Dia's African socialism ended in 1962.

notes.text: Plan quadriennal 1961–64 prepared with the French Dominican economist Louis-Joseph Lebret (IRFED).
notes.src: République du Sénégal (1961) Plan quadriennal de développement

notes.text: Fall of Mamadou Dia; the cooperative programme is diluted.
notes.src: Gellar, S. (1982) Senegal: An African Nation between Islam and the West

notes.text: Remains in the CFA franc zone throughout.
notes.src: BCEAO

CIV.summary: The closest continuation of the French model: indicative plans, French advisers in ministries and the CFA franc.

notes.text: Perspectives décennales de développement 1960–1970 under Houphouët-Boigny.
notes.src: Ministère du Plan, Perspectives décennales

notes.text: French technical assistants staff key ministries.
notes.src: Zartman, I. W. and Delgado, C. (1984) The Political Economy of Ivory Coast

GIN.summary: The sharpest break with France: a 'No' vote in 1958, exit from the franc zone and a Soviet-bloc planned economy.

notes.text: Guinea rejects the French Community; French personnel withdraw.
notes.src: Referendum of 28 September 1958

notes.text: Own currency outside the franc zone; three-year plan with Eastern-bloc aid.
notes.src: Plan triennal 1960–63

notes.text: Conté government begins liberalisation with the IMF.
notes.src: IMF Guinea programmes, 1986

DZA.summary: French planning forms filled with a Soviet-style industrial strategy, designed partly by the French economist Destanne de Bernis.

notes.text: Autogestion (self-management) of abandoned settler estates.
notes.src: March decrees, 1963

notes.text: Triennial and four-year plans built on 'industrialising industries' and hydrocarbons.
notes.src: de Bernis, G. D. (1971) Les industries industrialisantes et les options algériennes, Tiers-Monde 47

notes.text: IMF stand-by and structural adjustment.
notes.src: IMF Algeria programme (1994)

TUN.summary: French administrative planning; a cooperative socialist experiment in the 1960s, then gradual liberalisation.

notes.text: Perspectives décennales 1962–71 under Ahmed Ben Salah; agricultural cooperatives expanded.
notes.src: République tunisienne (1962) Perspectives décennales

notes.text: Cooperative programme abandoned; Ben Salah dismissed.
notes.src: Bellin, E. (2002) Stalled Democracy

MAR.summary: French-style plans and a mixed economy under the monarchy, with Moroccanisation in 1973 and adjustment from 1983.

notes.text: Plan quinquennal 1960–64 under Abderrahim Bouabid.
notes.src: Royaume du Maroc (1960) Plan quinquennal

notes.text: Moroccanisation decree transfers foreign-owned firms and land.
notes.src: Dahir of 2 March 1973

notes.text: Structural adjustment with the IMF and World Bank.
notes.src: IMF Morocco programmes (1983)

AGO.summary: Independence in war; the MPLA adopted Marxism-Leninism and central planning with Soviet and Cuban support, alongside an oil enclave.

notes.text: MPLA First Congress declares a Marxist-Leninist programme.
notes.src: MPLA (1977) Orientações Fundamentais

notes.text: Programa de Saneamento Económico e Financeiro begins the market turn.
notes.src: Government of Angola (1987) SEF

MOZ.summary: FRELIMO's socialist central planning after 1977, reversed by the 1987 rehabilitation programme with the World Bank and IMF.

notes.text: FRELIMO Third Congress adopts Marxism-Leninism.
notes.src: FRELIMO (1977) Third Congress documents

notes.text: Indicative Prospective Plan (PPI) for a decade of development.
notes.src: Plano Prospectivo Indicativo (1981)

notes.text: Programa de Reabilitação Económica with the IMF and World Bank.
notes.src: Government of Mozambique (1987) PRE
